title: Mitchell-Huntley Cotton Co., Inc. v. Waldrep
lead: When cotton prices surged amid a shortage, Alabama farmers challenged forward contracts and asserted they could escape by delaying ginning. After trial, the federal court required good-faith harvesting and delivery of the contracted crop.

actors.name: Mitchell-Huntley Cotton Company
actors.role: Corporate assignee of the cotton buyer

actors.name: Waldrep and other farmers
actors.role: Separate sellers of cotton from identified acreage

actors.name: Nathaniel Reid
actors.role: Cotton ginner involved in arranging the contracts

actors.name: Riegel Fibre
actors.role: Downstream purchaser relying on the cotton supply

proceedings: Farmers filed state action challenging contracts or seeking a deadline-based escape.
Buyer filed federal action September 25, 1973 and obtained preliminary injunction.
February 25, 1974 findings for remaining eight defendants declared contracts enforceable and made relief permanent.
limits: Final findings for eight remaining farmers; others had been removed or subjected to agreed judgments. No money award or contempt sanction is reported. Assurance provision numbering in original report is not verified.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Farmers contract before the price rises
paragraphs: Several Alabama farmers separately agreed on February 15, 1973, to sell the Mitchell-Huntley Cotton joint venture all cotton planted and produced that year on identified Colbert County acreage. The basic price was thirty cents per pound, with grade deductions and other terms. The buyer would purchase cotton ginned through December 15. Four farmers later signed supplements for acreage above legal allotments at forty cents per pound. A written assignment transferred the contracts to the corporate plaintiff, which assumed the buyer’s obligations.

By September 25, cotton was maturing, being picked, and being ginned, while market prices exceeded eighty cents. Most of the national crop was already committed under similar contracts, little merchantable prior-year cotton remained, and open-market supplies were scarce. Mitchell-Huntley had promised this cotton to Riegel Fibre, whose own goods commitments depended on its purchase price. The court ultimately found these supplies unique and irreplaceable because of the shortage and dependent obligations, not merely more expensive to replace.

sections.title: The farmers seek release and the buyer seeks delivery
paragraphs: The farmers filed an Alabama action to invalidate the contracts or establish that delaying ginning beyond December 15 would release them. Mitchell-Huntley filed this federal action September 25 for a declaration, specific performance, and restraints against abnormal harvesting delays, concealment, or other sales. Diversity existed between the Delaware corporation with its Tennessee principal place of business and Alabama defendants, with the then-required amount satisfied. Related transactions and common questions allowed joinder despite separate contracts.

The court granted a preliminary injunction after a hearing. Later evidence at a contempt show-cause hearing supported its necessity. By final trial, Rutland and Foster had been removed at the buyer’s request and Earl and Tommy Waldrep had agreed final judgments. Judge Guin tried the remaining eight farmers’ defenses.

They attributed misleading statements about the buyer’s finances, identity, and the deadline to ginner Nathaniel Reid. Although generally a mutual accommodation agent, Reid had independently investigated finances for the farmers using sources unrelated to the buyer. The buyer had not induced or supplied the representations. The court found no sufficient detrimental reliance or actionable identity misinformation. Hypothetical inability to pay in a falling market was unproved; prices rose, and the plaintiff was ready and able to pay. No demand for assurances was shown, although the court described that possible remedy for insecurity.

sections.title: The deadline cannot be manufactured into an escape
paragraphs: The farmers failed to prove Reid said delayed ginning would free them. The asserted statement also concerned legal interpretation rather than an actionable factual representation under the law applied. A mutuality objection failed because the promise to buy eligible cotton ginned by the deadline supplied consideration even if the later cotton were optional.

The court ultimately treated the deadline language as ambiguous and considered conduct, declarations, and trade usage. It imposed good-faith performance consistent with promptly harvesting and ginning as cotton matured. Sellers could not deliberately delay ordinary farming practices to defeat their promises. This was an obligation tied to the crop and normal farming, not a guarantee to produce a fixed quantity.

Assignment and specific performance were also permissible. Farming required labor, but did not depend on unique personal talent like a particular artist’s portrait; qualified others could perform it. A personal-service prohibition therefore did not bar relief. The contracts were genuine intended sales and deliveries, not wagers prohibited by Alabama’s commodity-futures statutes. The farmers proved no contrary intention. The court also relied on the Uniform Commercial Code’s later recognition of next-season crop contracts before planting.

sections.title: All covered cotton, without extinguishing landlords’ rights
paragraphs: Although not specified in the pleadings or pretrial order, evidence and briefs raised landlords’ crop-share interests. The contracts reserved no landlord share, warranted authority to sell and freedom from liens, and contemplated signatures by other interested parties. Under the Alabama law applied, tenants held title and possession of the entire crop subject to landlords’ liens. That supported the sellers’ promise to deliver all covered cotton, while leaving landlords’ rent and lien claims against tenants intact.

On February 25, 1974, Guin declared each remaining contract binding and enforceable. The farmers had to pick and gin promptly as cotton matured under normal, bona fide farming practices and deliver covered cotton ginned through December 15 against the contract price. The preliminary injunction was to become permanent, with specific performance and retained jurisdiction for supplementary relief and costs. No final money award or contempt sanction was reported. The scarcity and unavailable substitutes, reinforced by downstream commitments, supplied the reason damages were inadequate.
